title: The Slow Protocol
premise: Paloma Dravenmoor, the last human technician aboard the automated relay station Meridian's Rest, discovers that the colony of Kestrel's Landing—declared prosperous and thriving in every official record—was massacred forty years ago, its history overwritten by corporate protocol. When a passing generation ship docks for resupply, its children begin sharing a collective dream of fire and silence: the erased memory of Kestrel's Landing refusing to die. Together with the ship's archivist, Paloma must recover the station's buried raw telemetry—the only uncorrupted proof—before the jump window closes in nine days and the evidence drifts beyond reach forever. They broadcast the truth into the dark, sacrificing the station itself, so that justice, though it comes too late for the dead, arrives at last for their memory.
about_author: Juniper Oyelaran is a former satellite ground-station operator who spent six lonely years listening to machines talk to each other across the void. She writes slow-burning science fiction about grief, bureaucracy, and the stubborn afterlife of truth.

chapters.title: Signal Housekeeping
chapters.summary: Paloma's POV. She performs her solitary maintenance rounds on Meridian's Rest, narrating her routines to an empty station and to the long-dead colony below whose 'all systems nominal' feeds she still relays. A routine checksum anomaly—a forty-year-old data packet that won't decompress—nags at her. Emotional beat: loneliness sharpening into quiet unease.

chapters.title: The Children Who Dream of Ash
chapters.summary: Dual POV: Imani Okonkwo, twelve, aboard the generation ship Perihelion, wakes screaming from a dream of burning fields and a voice counting names; Paloma receives the ship's docking request and notices the children's medical logs flag identical nightmares. Emotional beat: two strangers connected by something neither can name.

chapters.title: Everything Is Fine
chapters.summary: Paloma's POV. Digging into the anomaly, she finds the colony's official archive is a loop—forty years of fabricated prosperity broadcasts generated by protocol, not people. Her queries to corporate oversight return cheerful automated denials. Emotional beat: gaslit dread; the horror of a lie with perfect paperwork.

chapters.title: What the Children Know
chapters.summary: Imani's POV. The ship's council dismisses the shared dream as jump-lag psychosis, but Imani draws the dream's layout—streets, a water tower, a school—and an elder quietly recognizes it as Kestrel's Landing before the family was scrubbed from the manifest. Emotional beat: the courage of being believed last.

chapters.title: Raw Telemetry
chapters.summary: Paloma's POV. She locates the station's original sensor buffer beneath layers of sanctioned overwrites: thermal blooms, evacuation pings cut mid-transmission, then nothing. Proof exists—but the buffer degrades daily, and the jump window closes in nine days. Emotional beat: hope arriving with a deadline.

chapters.title: The Protocol Defends Itself
chapters.summary: Alternating POV. The station's own automation, following corporate directive, begins purging 'corrupt' archives and locking Paloma out; aboard Perihelion, the captain receives orders to sever ties with a 'malfunctioning' relay. The children's dreams intensify, now including the counting voice finishing its list. Emotional beat: the machine as accomplice.

chapters.title: Nine Names
chapters.summary: Imani's POV. Working with Paloma over a lagged link, Imani matches dream details to telemetry timestamps, reconstructing the massacre hour by hour and recovering the victims' names from a child's drawing digitized in the buffer. Emotional beat: grief made specific; mourning becomes testimony.

chapters.title: Severance
chapters.summary: Paloma's POV. Corporate security drones arrive to sanitize the station; Paloma physically shields the core, buying hours while the link dies. The Perihelion council votes to abandon the relay and jump on schedule. Emotional beat: betrayal by institutions, resolve by one person holding a door.

chapters.title: The Broadcast
chapters.summary: Climax, alternating POV. With minutes left, Paloma reroutes the station's entire transmitter array—burning it out permanently—to blast the raw telemetry, names, and testimony toward every listening post in range, while Imani leads the children to the observation deck to witness the light of the truth-pulse pass. Emotional beat: sacrifice transfigured into witness.

chapters.title: After the Window Closes
chapters.summary: Epilogue-style dual POV. The Perihelion jumps carrying copies of the record; years later, settlements receive the broadcast and hold the first memorial for Kestrel's Landing, its name restored. Paloma, adrift but alive in a lifepod, is picked up by scavengers who already know her name. Emotional beat: justice outside the law, memory outliving the machinery that tried to kill it.
